opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the frontier has shifted quite a bit over the last couple of years. For a long time the story was mostly about scale: more parameters, more tokens, more compute, and you'd get predictable improvements. That's still true to some extent, but the interesting questions now are elsewhere.

The first big one is data. We've largely gone through the high-quality text available on the web, so the question becomes how you get more signal out of what you have and how you generate new data that's actually useful. Synthetic data is a big part of that, but it's tricky. If you're not careful you just distill the model's own biases back into itself. Where it works really well is in domains where you can verify the output, like math and code. You can check whether a proof goes through or a program passes its tests, and that gives you a clean training signal you can scale almost indefinitely.

That connects to the second area: reasoning and reinforcement learning on top of pretraining. A lot of the recent gains haven't come from the pretraining phase but from teaching models to think longer, explore, backtrack, and use feedback from verifiers. I spent a lot of time on theorem proving and symbolic math, and what's exciting is that ideas that felt niche a few years ago, like search over reasoning steps and formal verification, are becoming central to how we build general models.

Third is efficiency. Not everyone has unlimited compute, and I think there's a lot of room left in architecture choices, mixture-of-experts, better tokenization, longer and cheaper context, and inference-time efficiency. As models do more reasoning at test time, inference cost matters as much as training cost, so the design trade-offs change.

And finally, evaluation. Honestly, it's one of the hardest problems. Benchmarks saturate very quickly and contamination is everywhere, so knowing whether you've actually made progress is getting harder. I think whoever builds better ways to measure real capability, especially on long, open-ended tasks, will have a real advantage in steering research.

So if I had to summarize: less "just make it bigger" and more about data quality, verifiable feedback, reasoning, and efficiency. That's where I think most of the interesting work is right now.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. Honestly, I think the frontier has moved away from the thing people spent years obsessing over, which was just scaling pretraining. Not that scale stopped mattering, but the marginal return on another order of magnitude of raw web text is clearly not what it was in 2022 or 2023. We've more or less exhausted the easy supply of high-quality human text, so the question becomes: where does the next unit of capability come from?

For me there are three places. The first is data, but data in a very different sense than before. It's less about crawling more and more about generating, filtering, and verifying. Synthetic data works extremely well when you have a verifier, so code and math are the obvious cases, and that's exactly why those domains progressed so fast. The hard research problem is extending that to domains where there is no clean verifier. How do you get a reliable reward signal for a long report, a scientific argument, a design decision? That's where I think a lot of the interesting work is.

The second is post-training with reinforcement learning, which went from being a small alignment step to being a huge part of the compute budget. We are now training models that spend a lot of tokens thinking before they answer, and the training signal comes from outcomes rather than imitation. It's still early. We don't really understand the scaling laws there, we don't know how to make exploration efficient, and we are often bottlenecked by environments rather than compute. Building good environments, especially agentic ones with tools and long horizons, is almost an engineering discipline of its own now.

And the third is efficiency, which I think is underrated by people who only look at the top of the leaderboards. At Mistral we always cared about this because we didn't have the biggest clusters. Sparse mixture of experts, better attention variants, distillation, quantization-aware training, all of that compounds. If you can get the same capability at a tenth of the inference cost, that changes what people actually deploy, and deployment is what feeds data and feedback back into the loop.

If I had to summarize, I'd say the frontier is no longer "a bigger model on more text." It's the whole loop: environments, verifiers, RL, and the systems work that makes it affordable. The labs that figure out how to close that loop in open-ended domains will be the ones that matter in the next few years.

astra-6.text:
I think one of the most interesting questions is how to move beyond learning only from a fixed collection of human-written text. Pretraining has been incredibly effective, but we also want models that can try something, get feedback, and improve from that feedback.

Math and code are particularly interesting because you can often verify the result. If a model writes a program, you can execute it. If it produces a formal proof, you can check it. That gives you a learning signal that doesn’t depend entirely on a human judging whether an answer looks convincing. The challenge is making that process produce genuinely new capabilities, rather than just reinforcing things the model already knows how to do.

There’s also a closely related question around inference: how do you let a model use more computation on a difficult problem, and make that additional computation useful? Generating a longer answer is not necessarily the same as reasoning better. You need ways to explore alternatives, recognize mistakes, and decide which steps are worth pursuing.

So I would say the frontier is partly in scaling training, but also in building a better loop between generating solutions, checking them, and learning from the results. The harder question is how far we can extend that beyond domains where verification is straightforward.

r001.rationale: The response discusses feedback-based training and useful inference-time computation, but does not mention rewards taking hours or a challenge caused by divergence between the trajectory-generating model and the model being updated.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one of the biggest questions is how to move beyond learning only from a fixed dataset. Pretraining has been incredibly effective, but we want models that can tackle a problem, get feedback, and use that feedback to improve. That makes reasoning, reinforcement learning, and the quality of the training signal very interesting areas.

There’s also a lot to understand about efficiency. If a model gets a better result by spending more time thinking, how do you train it to spend that compute productively? How does it know when to explore another approach or check its answer? I think the frontier is increasingly about the interaction between training and inference, rather than treating them as two completely separate stages.
